items.title: 1. Build projects that solve problems companies actually have.
items.quote: 1. Build projects that solve problems companies actually have. Stop building random tutorial projects that nobody would use. Read engineering blogs, research real problems companies are solving, and better yet, build something relevant to the company you're applying to. items.title: 2. Use as much AI as you want, but understand your code.
items.quote: 2. Use as much AI as you want, but understand your code. I don't care how much of your code was written by AI. But if I ask why you chose a particular architecture, library, or approach, you should be able to explain it. You don't need to memorize every line, but you should understand the decisions behind it.

items.title: 3. Show your engineering decisions, not just your final code.
items.quote: 3. Show your engineering decisions, not just your final code. A small, well documented project is far more impressive than a massive repository. Write a short Markdown file explaining your architecture, tradeoffs, what didn't work, and what you'd change. If you built multiple iterations, include a simple changelog. Let me see how you thought through the problem.

items.title: 4. Make it ridiculously easy to run your project.
items.quote: 4. Make it ridiculously easy to run your project. You'd be surprised how many repositories I've tried to run that simply don't work. Include clear setup instructions, working dependencies, and ideally a live demo or API. Assume the person interviewing you will actually clone and run your code. Because I often do.

items.title: 5. Show me that you've actually tested what you built.
items.quote: 5. Show me that you've actually tested what you built. What edge cases did you test? What are the known limitations? Even a handful of meaningful tests tells me you've thought beyond generating code. AI has made it incredibly easy to build things that would've taken teams of engineers a few years ago. But it's also made it easy to create the appearance of engineering work without much engineering thinking.
